Boris Vujčić: Interview with Kurier
body: What is the value of the euro and the euro area in uncertain times like these?

Vujčić: The value of the euro area and the euro is particularly high for a country during times of crisis. We’ve seen this over the years. In times of great uncertainty, during crises, when yields and spreads are rising or there are tensions in financial markets, the real benefits of the euro become very clear. I can tell you this, because I was in charge of the monetary policy of a small, open economy close to the euro area for 25 years. In good times, it made less difference whether a country was in the euro area or not. It’s in times of crisis that the difference was stark.

Kocher: The euro is particularly valuable for Austria as an open and highly export-oriented economy. The single currency facilitates trade and investment, eliminates exchange rate risks within the euro area, and provides a reliable framework for businesses and households. In times of economic and geopolitical uncertainty, being part of a strong monetary union is a major advantage. The euro also gives Europe greater weight on the international stage.

Vujčić: There are a few examples – from the global financial crisis, the euro sovereign debt crisis and the pandemic. Just before Croatia joined the European exchange rate mechanism, the currency market was under such pressure in the spring of 2020 that it was really difficult to keep the exchange rate stable. That’s when we entered into a swap agreement with the European Central Bank (ECB). As soon as that was in place, the market upheaval calmed down. This is a clear example of how important the euro can be. Access to a swap line in such a situation acts as a shield. In effect, we went from a high-pressure situation where we had to make significant market interventions and deal with ballooning interest rates to a much more stable phase. Thanks to that transition, we were able to adjust our other economic policy measures to deal with the challenges of the pandemic.
The euro has weakened markedly since the beginning of the year. Why is that?

Vujčić: I wouldn’t use words like “weak” or “strong”. I think that the euro is moving within a certain historical fluctuation range against the US dollar – as that is the relevant benchmark here. The euro initially gained, then lost value somewhat. But it’s still stronger than it was a few months after its introduction, for example. This is why I don’t think that speaking of “weak” is necessarily accurate. The exchange rate typically follows monetary policy expectations and as such the interest rate differential between the United States and the euro area, as well as other economic fundamentals.

Kocher: There is strong demand for a new programme launched by the ECB, called EUREP 2.0. It consists of repo agreements concluded with central banks. This means that the euro is in high demand outside the euro area too. There is growing international interest in the euro as a safe currency, including beyond Europe’s borders.
How stable is the euro in the context of budget problems in France?

Vujčić: As we often emphasise, fiscal issues must be solved with fiscal measures. I think that this is now well understood in France too. However, we are in the lead-up to an election now. Typically, in such periods no major decisions are made. These tend to be postponed until after elections. But I believe that France will then be ready to deal with these problems. I also expect the budget which is important now to be passed before the year-end and probably remain in place until after the summer next year.
Isn’t there a risk that we end up with the same kind of problem we had close to 15 years ago with Greece?

items.t: Decisions taken by the Governing Council of the ECB (in addition to decisions setting interest rates)
body: Agreement for Sweden to join T2

On 25 November 2026 the ECB announced that it had concluded an agreement with Sveriges Riksbank for Sweden to join T2, the Eurosystem’s real-time gross settlement system. More information is available in the press release issued at the occasion of the signing ceremony with ECB President Christine Lagarde and Sveriges Riksbank Governor Erik Thedéen of the T2 currency participation agreement.
Acceptance of marketable assets issued on distributed ledger technology (DLT) platforms licensed under the EU DLT Pilot Regime as Eurosystem collateral

On 19 November 2026 the Governing Council approved the acceptance of marketable assets issued on DLT platforms licensed under the EU DLT Pilot Regime Regulation (EU) 2022/858 and reachable via TARGET2-Securities (T2S) as eligible collateral for Eurosystem credit operations, subject to specific Eurosystem requirements. This decision is part of a roadmap exploring ways to expand eligibility to assets issued and settled entirely on DLT networks. The decision is due to take effect in June 2027 and is explained in a press release available on the ECB’s website. It follows the ECB announcement of 27 January 2026 that marketable assets issued in central securities depositories using DLT will be accepted as collateral. These decisions testify to the Eurosystem’s commitment to aligning its collateral framework with advances in technology, while upholding the principles of adequacy of collateral, safety, efficiency and a level-playing field.
Financial Stability Review – November 2026

On 12 November 2026 the Governing Council held an exchange of views on the basis of the November 2026 edition of the Financial Stability Review and authorised its publication on the ECB’s website. In addition to providing an overview of key financial stability vulnerabilities in the euro area, this edition includes three special features. The first discusses the financial stability implications of AI adoption in the real economy and the financial industry. The second explores the complex interplay between AI and cybersecurity. The third assesses the financial stability implications of large initial public offerings and equity issuance in general, as well as how they both interact with the trend towards passive investing. The Financial Stability Review was published on 18 November 2026 on the ECB’s website, together with a related press release.
2026 study on payment attitudes of consumers in the euro area

On 12 November 2026 the Governing Council took note of the results of the 2026 study on the payment attitudes of consumers in the euro area and approved its publication on the ECB’s website. The results show that consumers are increasingly using digital means of payment, while cash continues to play an important role. Moreover, while payment practices are changing, consumers’ own preferences nonetheless remain stable. The results of the study, together with a related press release, are available on the ECB’s website.

ECB Consumer Expectations Survey results – October 2026
body: In October the median rate of perceived inflation over the previous 12 months increased to 4.1% from 3.6% in September and stood at its highest level since July 2024. Median expectations for inflation over the next 12 months also rose to 3.5% from 3.1%, but remained below the level reached at the start of the conflict in March 2026 (4.0%). Median expectations for inflation three years ahead increased to 3.0% from 2.9%, returning to the March 2026 level. Median expectations for inflation five years ahead were unchanged at 2.5% for the third consecutive month, the highest level since the start of the series in August 2022. Uncertainty about expectations for inflation over the next 12 months increased for the second consecutive month, remaining higher than the level prior to the start of the conflict in the Middle East. Respondents in the bottom income quintile continued to report higher inflation perceptions and expectations, on average, than those in the top quintile. Younger respondents (aged 18-34) continued to report lower inflation perceptions and expectations than older respondents (aged 35-54 and 55-70).

Consumers’ expectations for nominal income growth over the next 12 months fell to 0.6% from 1.1% in September. While expectations declined across all income quintiles, the decline was most pronounced in the bottom income quintile (by 0.7 percentage points to 0.8%) and in the top quintile (by 0.8 percentage points to 0.4%). Perceived nominal spending growth over the previous 12 months increased to 5.4% from 5.3% in September, while expected nominal spending growth over the next 12 months was unchanged at 3.7%.

Expectations for economic growth over the next 12 months increased in October to -1.3% from -1.5% in September. Expectations for the unemployment rate 12 months ahead decreased to 11.0% from 11.3% in September. As observed in previous months, households in the bottom income quintile expected the highest unemployment rate 12 months ahead (13.3%), while households in the top income quintile expected the lowest rate (9.5%). Consumers continued to expect the future unemployment rate to be only slightly higher than the perceived current unemployment rate (10.4%), suggesting a broadly stable labour market outlook. Quarterly data revealed a somewhat mixed labour market sentiment. Unemployed respondents reported a lower expected probability of finding a job over the next three months, at 29.6% in October compared with 30.8% in July. Employed respondents reported a lower expected probability of job loss over the next three months, at 9.4% in October compared with 9.8% in July.

Consumers expected the price of their home to increase by 3.3% over the next 12 months, lower than in September (3.5%). As in previous months expectations for home price growth over the next 12 months remained, on average, higher in the lowest income quintile (3.8%) than in the highest income quintile (3.0%). Expectations for mortgage interest rates in 12 months’ time remained unchanged from July, at 4.9%. As in previous months, households in the top income quintile expected the lowest mortgage interest rates 12 months ahead (4.6%), while those in the bottom quintile expected the highest rates (5.4%). The net percentage of households reporting a tightening (relative to those reporting an easing) of access to credit over the previous 12 months increased compared with September. The net percentage of households expecting tighter credit conditions over the next 12 months (relative to those expecting an easing) also increased compared with September, reaching its highest value since October 2023. Quarterly data showed that the share of consumers who reported having applied for credit during the past three months increased slightly to 14.4% in October, from 14.3% in July.
The release of the Consumer Expectations Survey (CES) results for November is scheduled for 7 January 2027.

Meeting of 28-29 October 2026
body: Ms Schnabel started her presentation on the latest financial market developments with the observation that higher energy prices since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 9-10 September 2026 had reinforced concerns about persistent inflationary pressures. At the same time, market attention had shifted towards fiscal dynamics and concerns about the increasingly debt-financed artificial intelligence (AI) investment cycle.

Energy price pressures had intensified substantially since the September meeting, pushing oil and gas prices above the adverse scenario of the September 2026 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area. In response to renewed tensions in the Middle East, the latest oil futures curve had shifted markedly higher compared with the baseline of the September projections and had also moved visibly above the adverse scenario over the short term. The repricing in gas markets had been even more pronounced, with the futures curve currently standing well above the adverse scenario over the entire horizon.

Diesel refining margins stood at a historically high level, with euro area diesel crack spreads – the differences between wholesale prices and crude oil prices – above the levels observed after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Freight rates from the Gulf region to Europe had surged to record highs, while the probability of a US-Iran peace deal by the end of 2026 was at its lowest since the start of the war in the Middle East. The increase in energy prices was reflected in inflation compensation. Inflation fixings throughout 2026 and 2027 had shifted higher, peaking at 4.5% for January 2027 and remaining above 2.5% until the first quarter of 2028, while inflation fixings for 2028 were broadly unchanged. Option-implied inflation risks continued to be skewed to the upside over the next two years and five years.

Despite the sharp increase in energy prices and the deterioration in the inflation outlook, expectations for the key ECB interest rates stood near their September levels. The one-year overnight index swap (OIS) rate one year ahead had decoupled from energy prices, consistent with communication that interest rates would not move in lockstep with energy costs. Immediately after the Governing Council’s September monetary policy meeting, the OIS forward curve had shifted markedly higher, temporarily pricing in more than four additional 25 basis point hikes over the next 12 months, before investors pared back expectations to just under three additional hikes. Market pricing adjusted for term premia pointed to an expected peak in the deposit facility rate at around 3%, implying a more pronounced tightening than the median expectation of participants in the Survey of Monetary Analysts, which foresaw only one more hike.

Euro area risk-free rates had stabilised and, at longer tenors, had even declined since the September meeting, while US rates had risen across maturities on the back of higher real rates. The divergence between real yields in the euro area and the United States was consistent with investors’ perceptions of a more dynamic US economy.

The rise in euro area ten-year rates relative to the average in 2024 had been driven primarily by higher real term premia, reflecting increased uncertainty about the long-run macroeconomic outlook and a growing net supply of public and private debt. Higher expected short-term real rates and higher inflation expectations accounted for around one-third of the increase in ten-year rates. Moreover, the shift in stock-bond correlations into positive territory pointed to reduced diversification benefits from bonds amid more frequent adverse supply shocks, requiring greater compensation to hold duration risk.

Agencies announce dollar thresholds for applicability of truth in lending and consumer leasing rules for consumer credit and lease transactions
body: The Federal Reserve Board and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau today announced the dollar thresholds used to determine whether certain consumer credit and lease transactions in 2027 are subject to certain protections under Regulation Z (Truth in Lending) and Regulation M (Consumer Leasing).

By law, the agencies are required to adjust the thresholds annually based on the annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W. Transactions at or below the thresholds are subject to the protections of the regulations.

Specifically, based on the 3.9 percent annual percentage increase in the CPI-W as of June 1, 2026, Regulation Z and Regulation M generally will apply to consumer credit transactions and consumer leases of $76,300 or less in 2027. However, private education loans and loans secured by real property, such as mortgages, are subject to Regulation Z regardless of the amount of the loan.

items.t: ECB and Sveriges Riksbank conclude agreement for Sweden to join T2
body: The European Central Bank (ECB) and Sveriges Riksbank have concluded an agreement for Sweden to join T2, the Eurosystem’s real-time gross settlement system. Today, ECB President Christine Lagarde and Sveriges Riksbank Governor Erik Thedéen took part in a signing ceremony for the T2 currency participation agreement at the ECB.
This agreement will enable Sveriges Riksbank to use T2 for settling large-value payments in Swedish kronor. Migration is targeted for February 2030.

Joining T2 will move Sweden’s large-value payment settlement from a national platform to shared European infrastructure. Sveriges Riksbank and Swedish financial institutions will benefit from investments in security, resilience and technological development that are shared across participating markets, as well as from common European standards. Payments will continue to be settled in Swedish kronor using central bank money.

“Shared payment infrastructure strengthens Europe’s strategic autonomy and supports a more integrated financial system,” said ECB President Christine Lagarde. “This agreement builds on our partnership with Sveriges Riksbank and our joint commitment to safe and efficient payments.”

“By connecting to the European T2 platform for settling payments in Swedish kronor, we can, together with the ECB and other central banks, ensure that the Swedish settlement system becomes an even safer and more efficient payment system in the long run, both in everyday life and in a crisis,” said Sveriges Riksbank Governor Erik Thedéen.

TARGET Services are the Eurosystem’s financial market infrastructure for settling large-value payments, instant payments and securities transactions, and for managing collateral. In addition to payments in euro, T2 already supports large-value payments in Danish kroner. Both Sweden and Denmark use TARGET Instant Payment Settlement (TIPS) to settle instant payments in Swedish kronor and Danish kroner respectively.
Photos of the signing ceremony will be available on the ECB’s multimedia portal.

body: Real gross domestic product (GDP) increased at an annual rate of 4.3 percent in the third quarter of 2026 (July, August, and September), according to the second estimate released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). In the second quarter, real GDP increased 2.2 percent.

The contributors to the increase in real GDP in the third quarter were increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased.

Real GDP was revised up 0.9 percentage point from the advance estimate, primarily reflecting upward revisions to investment and consumer spending. For more information, refer to the "Technical Notes" below.

Compared to the second quarter, the acceleration in real GDP in the third quarter primarily reflected an acceleration in investment and an upturn in government spending that were partly offset by a downturn in exports. Imports increased more in the third quarter than in the second quarter.

Real final sales to private domestic purchasers, the sum of consumer spending and gross private fixed investment, increased 5.8 percent in the third quarter, revised up 0.9 percentage point from the previous estimate.

The price index for gross domestic purchases increased 2.7 percent in the third quarter, revised down 0.3 percentage point from the previous estimate. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index increased 2.1 percent, and the PCE price index, excluding food and energy increased 2.5 percent, both the same as previously estimated.

Real gross domestic income (GDI) increased 4.4 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 2.3 percent (revised) in the second quarter. The average of real GDP and real GDI also increased 4.4 percent, compared with an increase of 2.2 percent (revised).

Profits from current production (corporate profits with inventory valuation and capital consumption adjustments) increased $206.0 billion in the third quarter, compared with an increase of $384.0 billion in the second quarter.

items.t: Bowman, Modernizing Banking Supervision: A Shared Agenda for the Americas
items.x: Speech At the ASBA–BCBS–FSI High-Level Meeting for the Americas on Banking Supervision, Brasília, Brazil (via pre-recorded video)
body: Good morning.1 I would like to thank our hosts, the Banco Central do Brasil, the Association of Supervisors of Banks of the Americas (ASBA), the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), and the Financial Stability Institute, for bringing us together. Banking supervisors around the world are tasked with ensuring the safety and soundness of the banking system. To be effective in this work, bank supervisory and regulatory frameworks must be forward looking to anticipate future risks. Today, I will discuss three ways in which modernizing our supervision and regulatory frameworks can enhance our ability to be effective.

First, we must learn the appropriate lessons from failures of supervisory effectiveness. Recent experience in the United States demonstrates that it is not sufficient to identify financial risks. Supervisors must also have the authority, accountability, and judgment to act before those risks are realized.

Second, our regulatory and supervisory frameworks must be regularly revisited to keep pace with the evolving financial landscape. These frameworks must focus on the most material risks, enable timely decisions, and adapt to rapidly changing financial markets and technologies. This is a priority both for the Federal Reserve and our international colleagues, including those on the Financial Stability Board (FSB) and the BCBS.

Third, banking supervisors throughout the Americas must be effective. Our shared history, deeply interconnected economies, and regional financial challenges support alignment of our interests in maintaining strong institutions for supervisory cooperation. ASBA can play a role in that effort.

These points are closely related. Effective supervision requires sound judgment. Sound judgment must be supported by modern frameworks. And cooperation among supervisors in the Americas supports strengthening both.

Learning from Banking Failures: Information Must Lead to Action One of the most valuable responsibilities of any supervisory authority is to learn the right lessons from failure and adjust accordingly.

The March 2023 failure of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB), and subsequent discussions about what went wrong and paths for reform, provide a useful case study. Extraordinary measures were taken to address banking system stress in the wake of SVB's failure, and fundamental questions remain regarding the effectiveness of the Federal Reserve System's supervisory function. Earlier reviews of the bank's failure provided important information but did not consider questions about shortcomings in the Federal Reserve's supervisory approach or identify opportunities to address long-standing weaknesses in our supervision. When I became Vice Chair for Supervision, I initiated an independent review of SVB's failure.
The initial findings of that review released in September were sobering. The review validated that supervisors identified the bank's fundamental vulnerabilities well before its failure.2

Those vulnerabilities included substantial interest rate risk, a highly concentrated and predominantly uninsured deposit base, and inadequate preparedness to meet liquidity demands. These were not unfamiliar or complicated risks to understand. They have been common risks throughout history, were present at the time of SVB's failure, and continue to be fundamental banking risks today. Yet our supervisory process failed to produce timely and effective action to address them.

A central lesson is that the failure of supervision was not a failure to obtain information. It was a failure to translate information into timely, decisive action. The review identified a long-standing supervisory problem of consultation without conclusion or action, uncertainty about decisionmaking authority, and a lack of accountability. Supervisors identified concerns, documented weaknesses, and discussed vulnerabilities. But the process did not result in prompt action to require the bank to address material risks that ultimately led to its failure.

items.t: Card payments edge past cash in shops; euro area consumers want both
body: The European Central Bank (ECB) today published its latest study on the payment attitudes of consumers in the euro area (SPACE). The results show that consumers are increasingly using digital means of payment, while cash continues to play an important role.

For the first time since comparable data were collected in 2016,[1] cards were used more often than cash at physical locations, such as shops. In 2026 cards accounted for 45% of transactions, compared with 44% for cash. Mobile payments increased to 9%, from 6% in 2024.

While payment practices are changing, consumers’ own preferences remain stable. When paying in a shop, 54% preferred cards or other cashless methods, 22% preferred cash and 23% had no clear preference.

A large majority of respondents attach importance to retaining a choice of payment methods. For 82% of euro area consumers, it is important to have the option to pay digitally, while 62% value the option of paying with cash. Only 3% reported never using cash.

“Digital means of payment are becoming more important in day-to-day transactions, but choice is what really matters for Europeans,” said Piero Cipollone, member of the ECB’s Executive Board. “The ECB will continue to ensure citizens have the freedom to choose how to pay, by safeguarding cash while preparing for the possible issuance of its digital equivalent, the digital euro.”

Most consumers continue to find it easy to access cash, although the share declined to 85%, from 87% in 2024. Among those who had tried to withdraw cash from an ATM during the previous year, 19% experienced difficulties. In all euro area countries, at least 12% of consumers experienced non-acceptance of mobile or card payments at least once in the month preceding the survey.
The survey covered 51,551 respondents across the euro area. Data were collected in two rounds: the first between 29 September and 27 November 2025, and the second between 16 March and 15 May 2026.

items.t: Boris Vujčić: Resilience in an age of shocks: lessons from central and eastern Europe
body: This conference has long been associated with one of Europe’s most remarkable economic achievements: the convergence of the countries of central and eastern Europe (CEE).[1]

Since the mid-1990s, incomes in the region have more than doubled and the gap with advanced European economies has narrowed substantially (slide 2). EU accession and deeper integration into the Single Market were powerful forces behind this convergence, with openness being central to that success. Integration into European and global value chains supported productivity, while foreign direct investment accelerated capital accumulation and technology transfer.[2]

Yet the same openness that enabled convergence has also exposed CEE countries to repeated shocks. In the space of just a few years, Europe has faced a pandemic, Russia’s unjustified war against Ukraine, an unprecedented energy shock, disruptions to global supply chains and, more recently, renewed trade tensions and conflict in the Middle East.

These developments have placed economic resilience at the centre of the policy debate. And central and eastern Europe provides a particularly useful lens through which to think about what resilience means.

The experience of CEE economies provides valuable lessons for Europe as a whole. It shows us that openness and resilience are not opposites. In fact, integration can be a source of resilience through diversifying markets, suppliers and sources of financing. The question then is how to preserve the benefits of integration while strengthening our capacity to withstand and adapt to shocks.

So what actually makes an economy resilient? Resilience is not about avoiding shocks altogether – no economy can do that. Nor does it mean trying to become self-sufficient. Rather, resilience means having the buffers, institutions and flexibility to absorb shocks when they arrive, the capacity to recover afterwards and, ultimately, the ability to adapt to the new environment.
Today I would like to consider four dimensions of that resilience: monetary, fiscal, financial and structural.
Let me begin with monetary resilience.
The inflation shock that started in 2021 was an extraordinary test for central banks, reminding us that inflation can return unexpectedly and forcefully (slide 3).

And it was particularly significant in central and eastern Europe, where food and energy tend to weigh more heavily in household consumption baskets. Many economies in the region are also relatively energy-intensive, magnifying their exposure to the initial shock. Tight labour markets and strong wage growth subsequently contributed to domestic price pressures.[3]

Divergent inflation developments can require different monetary policy responses. For a small open economy outside the monetary union, this can also lead to exchange rate movements and shifts in capital flows and financing conditions, potentially amplifying the original shock.
Credible central banks can help contain these risks.

The experience of recent years reminds us why price stability is itself a source of resilience (slide 4). When inflation expectations remain anchored and people trust the central bank to fulfil its mandate, an external supply shock is less likely to turn into persistent inflation.
But credibility cannot be taken for granted. It has to be earned. And that requires central banks to act when circumstances demand it, even when the decisions involved are difficult.
There is also a broader lesson to be learnt from the region’s experience: monetary resilience depends on the monetary and financial structures in which economies operate.
Here, participation in the euro area can provide important benefits.

For a highly integrated economy, joining the euro area removes exchange rate risk from its interactions with its main trading and financial partners. It eliminates the possibility of currency movements amplifying a shock through balance sheets or financing conditions. And it gives the economy access to the institutions and common monetary framework of the euro area.
Croatia provides a useful illustration.

ECB expands acceptance of DLT-based assets as eligible Eurosystem collateral
body: The Governing Council of the European Central Bank (ECB) has approved the acceptance of marketable assets issued on DLT platforms licensed under the EU DLT Pilot Regime Regulation as eligible collateral for Eurosystem credit operations, subject to specific Eurosystem requirements. This is a new milestone in the roadmap towards making the Eurosystem collateral framework fit for a tokenised European financial market ecosystem, which entails exploring ways to accept and mobilise tokenised assets in their native form.

“We support innovation without lowering our standards”, says Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel. “A future-proof collateral framework must embrace new technologies without compromising on safety or the rigour of our risk assessment.”

The decision supports the expansion of the eligibility of DLT-based assets in the Eurosystem’s collateral framework through a measured, controlled and technology-neutral approach. At the same time, it ensures that the Eurosystem’s collateral framework remains robust, adaptable, future-proof and aligned with the Eurosystem’s broader work on tokenisation and Appia objectives.

To be eligible, the assets must meet all standard collateral eligibility criteria. The arrangements for mobilising these assets must comply with applicable Eurosystem requirements. This includes making the assets available to the Eurosystem via an eligible link to a central securities depository (CSD) operating an eligible securities settlement system. In line with the existing eligibility framework for Eurosystem credit operations, the securities settlement systems must comply with the Central Securities Depositories Regulation and offer settlement in the TARGET2-Securities platform. In addition to being licensed under the DLT Pilot Regime Regulation, DLT platforms will need to meet dedicated Eurosystem requirements to ensure legal certainty and operational safety regarding, for example, settlement finality designation and the outsourcing of critical functions. The Eurosystem expects to communicate the details of these requirements in the spring of 2027, with implementation planned to take effect in June 2027.

As stated by ECB Executive Board member Piero Cipollone, “Pontes and Appia are helping turn Europe’s vision for tokenised finance into reality. And by adapting our collateral framework, we are further enabling the European tokenised finance market to grow, while upholding the principles of safety, efficiency and a level playing field.”

Today’s decision follows the announcement on 27 January 2026 to accept as collateral assets issued in CSDs using DLT-based services. While the Eurosystem’s roadmap foresees further exploration of ways to expand eligibility to assets issued and settled entirely on DLT networks, today’s decision will significantly contribute to the interoperability between DLT platforms and traditional systems, thereby fostering integration in the current hybrid environment.

items.t: Federal Reserve announces College Fed Challenge winners
body: The University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) won the 23rd annual national College Fed Challenge on Friday, a team competition that encourages undergraduate students to learn about the U.S. economy, monetary policymaking, and the role of the Federal Reserve System. Teams analyze economic and financial conditions and formulate a monetary policy recommendation, modeling the Federal Open Market Committee. The team, from Los Angeles, California, represented the San Francisco District and included Aarushi Maheshwari, Annika Chan, Atul Prasanth, Caitlyn Cox, Finn Karish, Eli Brooks (alternate), Kennedy Yang (alternate), Manasi Vartak (alternate), Ronojoy Borpujari (alternate), and Sahil Sudani (alternate). The team's advisers were Chris Surro and Ali Haider Ismail.

"I am very happy to congratulate the students who competed in this year's College Fed Challenge, especially the winners and finalists," said Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh. "They took on the same big questions we policymakers face. I'm impressed by their talent, their rigor, and their eagerness to think hard about monetary policy and the economy."

This year's College Fed Challenge included 141 schools from 34 states across the nation, the most in the competition's history. Teams submitted video presentations or participated in local competitions last month. Twenty-one semi-finalist teams then participated in question-and-answer sessions held earlier this month, and seven finalists were invited to the Federal Reserve Board for the national finals. The other national finalists were the University of Chicago in second place and the University of Maryland, College Park in third place. Teams with honorable mentions include Cleveland State University, Harvard College, Pennsylvania State University, and St. Lawrence University.
Teams were evaluated on their economic analysis, responses to the judges' questions, teamwork, and presentations.

items.t: Cook, The U.S. Economy in Global Context
items.x: Speech At the XXIX Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile, Santiago, Chile
body: Thank you, Governor Costa, for that kind introduction and for the invitation to deliver this keynote address and to participate in the 29th Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile today.1 It is a distinct privilege to be back in Santiago. I first came to Chile between my second and third years as a Ph.D. student at Berkeley after completing a summer as an intern at the World Bank. I was on a quest to determine whether economic growth in Latin America or in another region of the world would be the subject of my dissertation. It piqued my interest in inflation targeting, a sound fiscal framework, and now, of course, how to think about the economic forces reshaping the global economy. I am grateful for the chance to continue to learn from your experience and to share some of my own thinking.

I want to begin by acknowledging a fact that may seem obvious but is easy to overlook in the day-to-day work of setting monetary policy: The U.S. economy does not sit in isolation. As a member of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, my mandate is domestic—to promote maximum employment and price stability in the United States. But achieving that mandate requires that I pay careful attention to global developments, including economic and financial developments in Chile and across Latin America. The forces reconfiguring your economies are, in many cases, identical to the forces reconfiguring ours, even if they arrive on our respective shores somewhat differently.

Geopolitics and Trade Let me start with geopolitical events. Over the past several years, the global economy has absorbed a remarkable sequence of shocks. Russia's war in Ukraine disrupted energy and commodity markets worldwide. The conflict in the Middle East pushed up energy prices again this year, and experts have warned that damaged infrastructure and depleted inventories could keep oil prices elevated for an extended period. These are not simply North American concerns. Oil is a globally traded commodity, and a conflict that drives up the price of oil in Houston drives it up in Santiago, as well. The precise transmission differs across countries, depending on whether they are net energy importers or exporters, but few economies have been insulated.

A related story applies to trade. Over the past two years, the U.S. has raised tariffs on a wide range of imports, and considerable uncertainty remains about where tariff levels will ultimately settle. In the U.S., the effects of tariffs on inflation appear to have moderated, even as uncertainty about future trade policy persists. China, too, has increased trade restrictions, limiting exports of critical minerals for which it supplies a large fraction of the world's production. These minerals are a crucial input, and uncertainty is rising around the world about access to them. I raise this not to make a judgment about trade policy—that is not my role—but because such shifts inevitably reverberate across the global economy. When trade relationships between major economies are altered, other countries must decide how to respond: whether to deepen commercial ties elsewhere, reconfigure supply chains, or wait for greater clarity before committing to new investment. These are decisions playing out in boardrooms and finance ministries around the world right now, including, I suspect, in some of the economies represented in this room.

The Global AI Buildout The third global force I want to highlight—and the one I will spend the most time on—is the extraordinary buildout of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure now underway around the world.

body: Worldwide employment by U.S. multinational enterprises increased 0.9 percent to 44.2 million workers in 2024 (preliminary) from 43.8 million workers in 2023 (revised), according to statistics released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis on the operations and finances of U.S. parent companies and their majority-owned foreign affiliates.

Employment in the United States by U.S. parents increased 0.1 percent to 29.9 million workers in 2024. U.S. parents accounted for 67.6 percent of worldwide employment by U.S. multinational enterprises (MNEs), down from 68.1 percent in 2023. Employment abroad by foreign affiliates of U.S. MNEs increased 2.7 percent to 14.3 million workers and accounted for 32.4 percent of employment by U.S. MNEs worldwide.

U.S. parents accounted for 21.7 percent of total private industry employment in the United States in 2024, down from 21.9 percent in 2023. Employment by U.S. parents was largest in manufacturing, in “other industries,” led by transportation and warehousing, and in retail trade. Employment abroad by foreign affiliates was largest in India, Mexico, and the United Kingdom.

Worldwide current-dollar value added of U.S. MNEs increased 8.0 percent to $7.4 trillion in 2024. Value added by U.S. parents, a measure of U.S. parents’ direct contribution to U.S. gross domestic product, increased 8.5 percent to $5.7 trillion. U.S parents accounted for 21.8 percent of total U.S. private-industry value added, up from 21.2 percent in 2023. Foreign affiliate value added increased 6.5 percent to $1.8 trillion. Value added by foreign affiliates was largest in the United Kingdom, Ireland, and Canada.

Worldwide expenditures for property, plant, and equipment of U.S. MNEs increased 7.1 percent to $1.2 trillion. Expenditures by U.S. parents accounted for $968.7 billion, representing 36.5 percent of all U.S. private-business capital expenditures. Expenditures by foreign affiliates accounted for $216.2 billion.

Worldwide research and development (R&D) expenditures of U.S. MNEs increased 10.1 percent to $622.7 billion. U.S. parents accounted for expenditures of $536.5 billion, representing 69.6 percent of business R&D performed in the United States. Foreign affiliates accounted for expenditures of $86.2 billion.

Additional statistics on the activities of U.S. parent companies and their foreign affiliates, including sales, balance sheet and income statement items, compensation of employees, trade in goods, and more are available on BEA’s website. More industry detail for U.S. parents and more industry and country detail for foreign affiliates are also available on the website.

items.t: Waller, Opening Remarks
items.x: Speech At the 2026 College Fed Challenge Finals, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Washington, D.C.
body: Thank you, Robin, and welcome, students and teachers, to the Federal Reserve Board.1

We are gathered for the finals of the annual College Fed Challenge, a tradition begun 23 years ago under Chairman Alan Greenspan. The challenge is to prepare and present a monetary policy recommendation that will best promote the Federal Reserve's dual mandate of stable prices and maximum sustainable employment. Students on the seven teams that will compete today represent the University of California, Los Angeles; the University of Chicago; Cleveland State University; Harvard College; the University of Maryland, College Park; Pennsylvania State University; and St. Lawrence University.

Let me start by congratulating all of the students here today, and your faculty advisers, for advancing to the finals by winning preliminary rounds of the competition. A record 141 schools participated this year, from 34 states. It is incredibly gratifying to think of the number of young people motivated to learn about the Federal Reserve's role in promoting a healthy economy.

A few weeks from now, my colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) and I will be sitting at this same table, facing the same challenge you face today. Like you, we will be examining publicly available data on economic and financial conditions and will apply our understanding of how monetary policy influences those conditions to render our best judgment of the policy stance that best furthers the Fed's goals.

Crucial to that decision will be clearly explaining the Committee's actions and intentions to the public—the same task that you will face later this morning, when you present your recommendations to our judges. As I hope you have learned, clear communication is essential because monetary policy works to a considerable extent by influencing the public's view of current and future economic and financial conditions.

Monetary policy has evolved since this competition began in 2003. At that time, the FOMC relied on a single tool to influence financial conditions and the broader economy—it set a target for the federal funds rate. In the years since, the Committee expanded its toolkit with unconventional policy tools.

In an important way, the competition you will engage in today is very much like what the FOMC does at its meetings. On December 8, my 18 FOMC colleagues and I will each present our view of the economic outlook, and on December 9, our view of the proper stance of monetary policy. Before we express those views to the public, we communicate with each other, presenting evidence, testing hypotheses, and making arguments that will ultimately help us arrive at a consensus that is summarized in our postmeeting statement. Every monetary policy speech I give has its origins in this room, in the argument I make here, and the extent to which that argument holds up to what I hear from my colleagues. When I engage in the essential task of explaining monetary policy to the public, I am really doing the same thing that I do here at FOMC meetings. And very much what you will do today. Present the evidence. Make an argument. Persuade.

I hope your preparations for this event have added to your understanding of the economy and the Federal Reserve's role and perhaps will even spur some of you to pursue further study of economics and finance. Among the talented individuals who are participating in today's challenge, I hope there are some who may one day contribute to our understanding of the economy and the work of the Fed. But I hope that all of you have benefited from this experience by adding to your knowledge and developing research, analytical, and communication skills that will help you in whatever careers you choose.

items.t: Christine Lagarde: Acting in time
body: It is a pleasure to be back at this congress. This is the eighth time I have spoken here as President of the ECB, and it will sadly be the last.
In preparing for today, I reread those speeches. The topics have varied, from growth and inflation to capital markets and the Single Market.
But one concern runs through all of them: how to make Europe stronger, so that its prosperity is driven by its own strengths and less exposed to decisions taken elsewhere.

For many years, the challenges we discussed here were old ones. We had fallen short of our ambitions for the Single Market. Our growth relied too heavily on external demand for an economy of our size, and our competitiveness was slowly eroding.

Those challenges have not gone away. But in recent years, new ones have been layered on top. Dependencies that we once saw as a normal part of an open economy, from critical raw materials to technology, can now be used against us. That has made economic sovereignty a challenge in its own right.
The old challenges and the new ones have something in common.
Five centuries ago, Machiavelli compared the problems of states to a fever that, at the start, is “easy to cure but difficult to detect” and, in time, becomes “easy to detect but difficult to cure”.
Both kinds of challenge are of this sort. By the time everyone can see the need to act, the best time to act has usually passed.

Acting early, before the case is obvious, is one of the hardest things a policymaker has to do. It means paying a price up front for a distant pay-off. And if nothing goes wrong, those who acted can easily appear to have paid that price for nothing.
Today I would like to reflect on how Europe can still act early, drawing on how we have approached this at the ECB and on what I have learned along the way.

It is often said that Europe only moves in a crisis. Jean Monnet wrote that Europe would be forged in crises, and would be the sum of the solutions adopted for them. The idea was that Europe has a kind of in-built inertia that only a crisis can overcome.
My experience of the past seven years is that this is only partly true. Europe responds decisively to some crises and hesitantly to others.
When events convince us that the world has changed, we act. During my term, I have watched Europe break one taboo after another.

Before the pandemic, few believed that the EU would ever borrow on a large scale in its own name. But once we accepted that no country could recover on its own, we created a recovery fund financed by common debt to the tune of €800 billion.

Europe was also said to be unable to take its own security seriously. Yet when Germany concluded that it would have to take on more of its own defence, it made the biggest change to its defence spending in generations. At the European level, we also agreed on Security Action for Europe (SAFE), which offers up to €150 billion in loans for joint defence procurement. And after decades of neutrality, Finland and Sweden joined NATO.

Nor did many expect Europe to act as a geopolitical power. Yet it is now Ukraine’s largest supporter. And when it became clear that Europe would have to bear more of the cost, the countries ready to act found a new way to borrow together on Ukraine’s behalf, even though not every country was ready to take part. Hence the coalition of the willing.

What made these steps possible? In each case, the cost of inaction was there for all to see, and it was plainly greater than the cost of acting. Once we were convinced of that, our institutions did not hold us back.

Our difficulties arise when a crisis moves slowly. The cost of inaction is then just as real, but it is far less visible. It builds up a little each year, and no single moment forces a decision. Meanwhile, the cost of acting is certain and has to be paid straight away.
Both the old challenges and the new ones are of this kind.
Take capital markets. We have all agreed for more than a decade that Europe needs a capital markets union. But building it means taking on vested interests now, for gains that arrive years later.

items.t: Jefferson, Monetary Policy amid Frequent and Complex Shocks
items.x: Speech At the International Monetary Fund and Central Bank of Brazil Conference “A Quarter Century of Inflation Targeting in Latin America: Progress, Challenges, and the Road Ahead,” Brasília, Brazil
body: Thank you, Nigel, for that kind introduction, and thank you to the Central Bank of Brazil and International Monetary Fund for hosting this important conference.1 It is an honor to be here with my fellow panelists. Today, I will briefly discuss issues that are critical for central bankers around the world—that is, how to assess and confront economic shocks. I discussed these issues in more depth in a speech earlier this year at Stanford University.2

Shocks, by their nature, are difficult to predict and vary in length, but we are nonetheless very familiar with them. Just in the past few years, we have experienced a pandemic, a rapid rise in energy prices associated with geopolitical tensions, changes to trade policy, and a technological breakthrough. One way to classify shocks is to determine whether their initial effect is on the demand side or the supply side of the economy. Demand shocks affect spending by households, businesses, or the government without changing productive capacity. Supply shocks change productive capacity—what economists call "potential output"—by affecting the available supply of labor and capital or the productivity of those inputs. The nature and duration of these shocks influence the approach to monetary policymaking.

As a monetary policymaker in the United States, I must consider whether and how shocks impact both sides of our dual mandate—maximum employment and stable prices. When a shock moves the output gap and inflation in the same direction, our objectives are aligned, and policy actions taken to address one also support the other.3 When a shock pushes them in opposite directions, there is a tradeoff. The recent rise in oil prices tied to the conflict in the Middle East is an example of the latter. An energy price shock can push up inflation while weighing on real incomes and demand. The appropriate response depends on the relative costs of missing each objective and the balance of risks. When the recent energy price shock occurred, inflation in the U.S. was already above our 2 percent target. If inflation expectations risk becoming unanchored, a stronger reaction to inflation is warranted. If price pressures are contained, it may be prudent to prioritize downside risks to employment.

Shocks that affect both aggregate supply and aggregated demand but with differential timing are especially challenging for monetary policymakers. The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) represents such a shock. Business adoption of AI has risen considerably over the past two years.4 On the demand side, optimism about the technology has been boosting business investment in data centers, advanced computing equipment, and related products. On the supply side, AI is likely to automate some tasks and augment others, which could raise productivity and, in turn, the growth rate of potential output. Currently, the AI buildout is exerting upward pressure on demand and inflation. In the future, advancements in productivity could exert downward pressure on inflation while continuing to support growth. Labor market effects are relevant as well. AI could cause some job displacement, a meaningful challenge for affected households. Like many technological breakthroughs of the past, however, AI could lead to the creation of new jobs and new firms that we have not yet imagined.

Shocks do not arrive in a vacuum. Energy, trade, and AI shocks are all unfolding at once. My colleagues at the Fed and my peers around the world must weigh them simultaneously. Our task is to remain attentive to our respective mandates and to keep the stance of our policies appropriately calibrated to achieve those stated goals. For the U.S. economy, my goal is to restore price stability while maintaining a solid labor market. That outcome will help the economy grow according to its full potential.
Thank you, and I look forward to our discussion.
1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee or the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. Return to text

items.t: Barr, Investing in America’s Underserved Communities
items.x: Speech At Making Missing Markets: Catalyzing Capital and Igniting Innovation, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, New York, New York
body: Thank you to the New York Fed and the organizers of this conference for the opportunity to speak to you today.1 For two reasons I can think of, New York is an excellent place to discuss ways to increase investments in communities where incomplete or missing markets have resulted in less investment than needed. First, it makes sense to initiate a conversation about incentivizing private investment in the center of American finance. Second, New York has been successful over the past few decades in attracting investment in lower-income neighborhoods, reversing forces that once made parts of this city synonymous with urban decline. I first saw that for myself 30 years ago, touring the South Bronx with Treasury Secretary Bob Rubin, where public–private partnerships were building housing, creating businesses and jobs, and making streets safer, block by block. That progress has continued, and the strategies and partnerships we will be discussing today have been a major engine for that success.

The backdrop for community investment, of course, is the economy—how fast it is growing, how well it is creating jobs, and how well incomes are keeping up with the cost of living. So I will start with the economic outlook. Overall, the economy is strong, with low unemployment, solid consumer spending, and robust business investment. But inflation is too high, making it hard for American families to make ends meet. Many families are struggling. And that's why it is so important for the Fed to bring inflation back down to our target of 2 percent in a timely way. If the economy evolves as I currently forecast, I expect it will be appropriate to raise rates further to achieve that goal on behalf of the American people. Of course, I'll continue to monitor the incoming data, the evolving forecast, and the balance of risks in making that assessment.

Strong and sustainable communities are key to American prosperity. When a community is strong and resilient, people see a future there and invest in that future—they buy homes, shop locally, and start new businesses. When hard times hit resilient communities, people can weather the storm and bounce back in part because they believe that they and their communities will bounce back—that jobs and opportunities will return. That's why we at the Fed are committed to building stronger communities. And while economic activity and employment are continuing to grow for the country as a whole, not all families and communities are thriving. Far from it. Wealthier households are doing well, but middle- and lower-income households are struggling, and the economy is leaving some communities behind. Recent estimates are that 44 percent of Americans live in low-income communities, where a fifth or more of people live below the poverty line.2 These communities often lack sufficient investment in housing, business, and infrastructure.

The Fed's recent Survey of Consumer Finances confirms that the majority of households has very little wealth.3 And lower-wealth households are nearly four times as likely to say that they cannot rely on friends and family for financial help or provide that help themselves.4 Think about how that inability to help, or get help, can reverberate across a community. When jobs and opportunities lag in a community, it eats away at the ties that connect families and neighbors. The dignity of work is so key to how many people try to navigate these difficult times, yet in many communities, despite a strong economy, some people are finding it hard to find a good-paying job.

items.x: The value added of the outdoor recreation economy accounted for 2.3 percent ($704.2 billion) of current-dollar gross domestic product (GDP) for the nation in 2025. Across states and the District of Columbia, value added for outdoor recreation as a share of state GDP ranged from…
body: Today, the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis released new statistics measuring the outdoor recreation economy for the nation, all 50 states, and the District of Columbia. The new data show that the value added of the outdoor recreation economy accounted for 2.3 percent ($704.2 billion) of current-dollar gross domestic product (GDP) for the nation in 2025 (national table 2). Across states and the District of Columbia, value added for outdoor recreation as a share of state GDP ranged from 6.1 percent in Hawaii to 1.0 percent in the District of Columbia (state table 1).

Inflation-adjusted (“real”) GDP for the outdoor recreation economy increased 1.9 percent in 2025, compared with an increase of 2.3 percent for the overall U.S. economy, reflecting a deceleration from the 2.5 percent increase in 2024 (national table 1). In 2025, real gross output for the outdoor recreation economy increased 2.1 percent, compensation increased 4.6 percent, and employment increased 1.7 percent (national table 9).

Outdoor recreation employment increased in 43 states and the District of Columbia in 2025. The change in outdoor recreation employment ranged from 5.0 percent in Rhode Island, Kansas, and the District of Columbia to −1.1 percent in New Jersey and Alabama (BEA interactive tables).

Outdoor recreation by activity Outdoor recreation activities fall into three general categories: (1) conventional activities such as bicycling, boating, hiking, and hunting; (2) other activities such as gardening and outdoor concerts; and (3) supporting activities such as construction, travel and tourism, local trips, and government expenditures. In 2025, conventional outdoor recreation accounted for 29.2 percent of U.S. outdoor recreation value added, compared with 29.1 percent in 2024. “Other outdoor recreation” accounted for 19.3 percent of value added in 2025, compared with 19.1 percent in 2024. Supporting outdoor recreation accounted for 51.5 percent of value added in 2025, compared with 51.7 percent in 2024.
Additional highlights for value added by activity for 2025 include (state table 2):

Outdoor recreation by industry The outdoor recreation by industry data show the contributions of industries to the outdoor recreation economy, including their impact on value added, gross output, employment, and compensation.

For the nation, the arts, entertainment, recreation, accommodation, and food services industry group was the largest contributor to U.S. outdoor recreation in 2025, accounting for $179.5 billion, or 25.5 percent of current-dollar value added. At the state level, arts, entertainment, recreation, accommodation, and food services was the largest contributor to outdoor recreation value added in 25 states and the District of Columbia. The states with the largest contributions were California ($23.5 billion), Florida ($23.4 billion), and New York ($11.6 billion) (state table 3).

Retail trade was the second-largest industry group for the nation, at $166.5 billion, or 23.6 percent of value added, and was the largest industry group in 22 states. The states with the largest contributions were California ($19.5 billion), Texas ($14.6 billion), and Florida ($13.3 billion).

Transportation and warehousing was the third-largest industry group for the nation, at $86.4 billion, or 12.3 percent of value added, and was the largest industry group in Alaska. The states with the largest contributions were Florida ($12.8 billion), California ($10.8 billion), and Texas ($7.1 billion).

Annual update of outdoor recreation economic statistics Estimates for 2021 to 2024 were updated to incorporate newly available and revised source data. At the national level, gross output, value added, employment, and compensation reflect the results of the 2026 annual update of the National Economic Accounts, which include the National Income and Product Accounts and the Industry Economic Accounts. The state statistics now reflect these updated national data as well as the 2026 annual update of the Regional Economic Accounts and newly available and revised regional source data.
Previously published estimates are available in BEA’s Data Archive.

items.t: Boris Vujčić: Financial Stability Review - November 2026
Risks from AI valuations, fiscal imbalances and geoeconomic tensions weigh on financial stability outlook
body: The outlook for euro area financial stability is being shaped by risks stemming from artificial intelligence (AI) valuations, fiscal imbalances and geoeconomic tensions, according to the November 2026 Financial Stability Review, which is published today by the European Central Bank (ECB).

“Risks to euro area financial stability remain elevated, given persistent geoeconomic uncertainty and growing exposure to AI,” said ECB Vice-President Boris Vujčić. “Banks are well placed to withstand shocks, while vulnerabilities are more pronounced in certain non-banks where risks are growing and macroprudential safeguards are less developed.”

The euro area economy has continued to demonstrate resilience despite an energy shock, trade frictions and extreme weather events. Prolonged energy supply disruptions and persistent trade policy uncertainty could, however, test this resilience.

Enthusiasm about the transformational potential of AI has driven strong gains in global equity markets, despite some recent volatility. Current valuations rely on ambitious earnings expectations which could yet be challenged by financing concerns or by competition from cheaper AI models. Investment in AI infrastructure is increasingly funded through debt, such that a potential change in sentiment could spread losses from equity markets to bond markets.

In the euro area, elevated debt levels, growing sovereign borrowing needs and shifts towards more news-sensitive and leveraged investors in euro area sovereign bonds are increasing the risk of abrupt repricing episodes, although markets have continued to function in an orderly manner. Geoeconomic uncertainty, higher energy prices and weak economic growth could further strain public finances, allowing governments less room to respond to shocks.

Banks’ and non-banks’ exposures to AI financing and sovereign bonds leave them exposed to repricing risks. While bank asset quality remains sound, higher energy prices and weaker economic conditions could make it harder for households and firms to repay their debts. Closer links between banks and non-banks could spread and amplify shocks across the financial system.

The euro area banking sector is well positioned to absorb potential shocks, underpinned by strong profits, solid capital buffers and ample liquidity. Preserving bank resilience remains a key macroprudential priority, alongside addressing vulnerabilities related to liquidity and high levels of borrowing among some non-banks. Accelerating progress on the EU’s savings and investments union will also be essential to support economic growth and competitiveness while preserving financial stability.
